content: Marsh Labrador Tea, also known as Northern Labrador Tea or Wild Rosemary (scientifically referred to as Rhododendron tomentosum, previously Ledum palustre), is a flowering plant that belongs to the subsection Ledum within the large genus Rhododendron of the family Ericaceae. This plant is a low-growing shrub that typically reaches a height of 50 cm, although it can occasionally grow as tall as 120 cm. Its leaves are evergreen, measuring between 12 and 50 mm in length and 2 to 12 mm in width. The flowers are small and characterized by a five-lobed white corolla. These flowers are grouped together in corymbs that are 3 to 5 cm in diameter. The plant emits a strong fragrance, which serves to attract bees and other pollinating insects. In terms of its geographical distribution, Marsh Labrador Tea is found in northern latitudes across North America, including Greenland, Canada, and Alaska. In Europe, it grows as far south as Germany, and in Asia, it extends southward to northern China, Korea, and Japan. The plant thrives in peaty soils, shrubby areas, and tundra environments dominated by mosses and lichens. Historically, this plant has been used in traditional herbal medicine, as detailed under the broader topic of Labrador Tea. Additionally, during the Middle Ages, it was traditionally employed as a gruit (a mixture of herbs) in the brewing of beer. It is important to note that all parts of the plant contain toxic terpenes, which can affect the central nervous system and may induce aggressive behavior. Early symptoms of overdose include dizziness and motor disturbances, which can progress to spasms, nausea, and loss of consciousness. Furthermore, even the scent of the plant can cause headaches in some individuals.
